title: The Ruling That Reached Strive Masiyiwa on a Boston Hotel Phone
dek: Between a 1996 decree and the last day of 1997, Strive Masiyiwa kept Econet's licence fight going with his money almost gone.

story.event: Keeping the licence fight going from the 1996 decree to the December 1997 ruling
story.summary: After Zimbabwe's Supreme Court struck down the state telecoms monopoly in December 1995, a 1996 presidential decree stopped Strive Masiyiwa from operating Econet's network, and he sold his government-dependent businesses at a loss while the litigation went on. A 1997 tender went to the rival Telecel consortium; Masiyiwa sought judicial review, and on 31 December 1997 Justice Sandura overturned the award and declared Econet licensed.
paragraphs: In February 1996 Strive Masiyiwa had a single Econet base station transmitting over Harare, and he had to switch it off. Weeks earlier, in December 1995, Zimbabwe's Supreme Court had ruled that the state Posts and Telecommunications Corporation's monopoly breached the constitutional right to freedom of expression. Then a presidential decree made running a private cellular network a crime, punishable by two years in jail. When police arrived with PTC engineers, he later wrote, everything was already off.

What followed was nearly two years of not knowing. More than 80 per cent of his engineering projects were for government, he wrote, and he was told to drop telecoms or lose his other businesses. He sold the government-dependent companies within two weeks, for far less than they were worth: '10 years of my work was all gone.' His lawyers agreed to carry on even if he ran out of money, and many creditors forgave or deferred his debts; he went to see each one. 'My financial resources were almost gone,' he wrote. 'We still had almost two years to go.'

In December 1996 the court again ordered the minister to end the monopoly. A tender followed, and early in 1997 the licence went to Telecel, a consortium with ruling-party links. Masiyiwa says Econet, with equipment already standing, was ranked fourth of five. An affidavit later filed in the High Court said the tender board had recommended a joint award to Econet and Telecel before the Cabinet secretary directed it to Telecel alone. His lawyers sought a High Court review, armed with the evaluation committee's papers, seized under a court order.

The ruling came on the last day of 1997, while Masiyiwa was in Boston with his pastor, trying to raise money for a hospital. In the early hours he rang a colleague in Harare from the hotel phone and was told the courts were closed for the holidays. About half an hour later the colleague called back: Justice Sandura, recently promoted to the Supreme Court, was clearing his High Court cases. He overturned the award and declared Econet 'duly licensed'. Days later the duty judge refused to suspend the order. By then, he wrote, he was 'financially exhausted', with a whole network still to pay for.

quote.text: Bend thy back unto thy chief, thine overseer in the King's palace, for thine house dependeth upon his wealth, and thy wages in their season. How foolish is one that quarrelleth with his chief, for one liveth only while he is gracious.
quote.source_title: The Instruction of Ptah-Hotep and the Instruction of Ke'Gemni: The Oldest Books in the World, translated by Battiscombe G. Gunn (Wisdom of the East series, John Murray, London, 1906), Project Gutenberg eBook #30508
quote.connection: The vizier's warning came true almost word for word: Masiyiwa's livelihood did depend on the state, and the quarrel cost him ten years of work. Ptahhotep would call that folly. Masiyiwa paid the price anyway, and the old advice is no less true for it.

reflection: Most days Ptahhotep is right. You depend on people: a lab that agrees to try your work, a funder, a first customer. Keeping their goodwill is part of the job, not a failure of nerve. Masiyiwa's story is not an argument for picking fights. It shows what a fight can cost once you are in it: years, savings, a business, sleep. And he did not carry it alone. His lawyers agreed to keep going even if he could not pay, and his creditors waited.
If there is a disagreement you are weighing, two plain questions are fair. Is this worth what it will take? And who would be carrying it with you?
invitation: Name one disagreement you are carrying at work. Today, decide only whether it needs a fight or a conversation, and leave the rest of it until tomorrow.

sources.title: Strive Masiyiwa's Narration of Court Battles in Establishing Econet (reproducing his Facebook series 'My Five Year Battle To Set Up A Cell Phone Business', 20 February to 28 March 2014)
sources.publisher: Pindula, reproducing Strive Masiyiwa's official Facebook page
sources.supports: Masiyiwa's own account: the 18 December 1995 ruling; the Ericsson system and single base station over Harare in February 1996; switching off when police and PTC engineers arrived; over 80% of his projects being for government and the ultimatum; selling the businesses within two weeks ('10 years of my work was all gone'); lawyers continuing even if he ran out of money; creditors forgiving or deferring debts; 'My financial resources were almost gone. We still had almost two years to go.'; the December 1996 court order; the tender, Econet ranked fourth of five; the judicial review and court-ordered seizure of committee papers; Boston, the hotel phone, Justice Sandura's ruling declaring Econet 'duly licensed'; the duty judge refusing to suspend it; 'financially exhausted'.

sources.title: "Dealing With Corruption Is Simple, Just Say No" (cover story, February 2014)
sources.supports: Loss of government work once he went to court and the sale of his construction business Retrofit to stay afloat; the court ruling in his favour in December 1997.

sources.title: How one entrepreneur beat corruption (Corinna Schuler, 1 March 2000)
sources.supports: The presidential decree under emergency powers making a private cellular network illegal, with two years in jail for offenders; the court-ordered tender lost to Telecel; Econet licensed in 1997 after further court battles.

sources.title: Zimbabwe airport furore (30 May 1997)

sources.title: The right to communicate: The Internet in Africa (Sally Burnheim)
sources.supports: Independent confirmation that in Retrofit (Pvt) Ltd v Posts & Telecommunications Corporation the Zimbabwe Supreme Court ruled in December 1995 that the PTC monopoly violated section 20 of the Constitution (freedom of expression).

sources.title: Econet Wireless Zimbabwe celebrates 14th anniversary (L.S.M. Kabweza, 10 July 2012)
sources.supports: Econet's own dating of its licence to the High Court ruling of 31 December 1997, and the formal signing of the licence in July 1998.

cross_checks.claim: Zimbabwe's Supreme Court struck down the PTC monopoly on freedom-of-expression grounds in December 1995 (Masiyiwa gives 18 December 1995).
In 1996 a presidential decree made it illegal to operate a private cellular network, carrying a jail sentence.
Masiyiwa lost his government work and sold his businesses during the fight.
The 1997 tender went to the Telecel consortium rather than Econet.
The decisive ruling declaring Econet licensed came at the end of December 1997 (31 December 1997 in Harare).

research_notes: Court and dates: Masiyiwa's 2014 account says the High Court ruled for him in January 1994, the Supreme Court reversed that in June 1994, and a fresh constitutional application succeeded on 18 December 1995. He calls the court the 'Constitutional Court'; ARTICLE 19 and the law report citations (Retrofit (Pvt) Ltd v Minister of Information, Posts and Telecommunications 1995 (2) ZLR 422 (S)) describe the Supreme Court, which the edition uses. The law reports themselves could not be fetched. Some retellings (NYU Law 2017, Nehanda Radio 2026) say the Supreme Court granted the licence in 1997; Masiyiwa's account and Econet (via Techzim) place the decisive ruling in a High Court judicial review by Justice Sandura, who had just been promoted to the Supreme Court and was clearing his High Court cases. Masiyiwa dates it to the night of 30 December 1997 in Boston; Econet dates it to 31 December 1997; the time difference reconciles these, so the edition says 'the last day of 1997'. Tender award: Masiyiwa says 28 February 1997, Wikipedia's Joice Mujuru article says 24 March 1997, so the edition says 'early in 1997'. The fourth-of-five ranking and the court-ordered seizure of committee papers are Masiyiwa's account only; the Christian Science Monitor separately reports documents showing an official docked 20 per cent from Econet's score. Business sale: his posts say he sold his government-dependent businesses within two weeks after a 1996 ultimatum; Forbes Africa (2014) has him saying government contracts ended the day the case was filed and that he sold Retrofit to stay afloat. The edition follows the detailed written account and does not name Retrofit or date the sale more precisely than 1996. In the same Forbes Africa interview he says 'I never had a sense of struggle', which sits awkwardly beside his own posts about near-bankruptcy; the edition quotes only the posts. His account gives a large role to prayer and a dream in Boston; the dream is omitted. The Facebook series is not fetchable without login, so it is read through Pindula's full reproduction; the quoted lines were checked word for word against Nehanda Radio's 2014 republication of Part 10 (https://nehandaradio.com/2014/05/29/strive-masiyiwa-story-storm-lashing-house-part-10/). Launch details conflict (Techzim/Econet: licence signed July 1998; Nehanda Radio 2026: launch June 1998), so the story stops at the ruling. The ARTICLE 19 PDF names the Retrofit case, not Masiyiwa or Econet, so an automated name check on that source may not match. Quote: Ptahhotep section 31 was chosen because it counsels the opposite of Masiyiwa's choice; translator and 1906 date (John Murray, London, Wisdom of the East series) confirmed from the edition's front matter.
